Sourcey is the closest direct match I found for this combination of inputs. If its licensing and generated C reference output suit your project, it is the first tool I would evaluate. A MkDocs or Sphinx build is also plausible, but those alternatives require several components and an explicit MCP-to-documentation export step.

## Ranked options

### 1. Sourcey — the most direct integrated option

[Sourcey](https://github.com/sourcey/sourcey) advertises a single static documentation build combining OpenAPI, MCP, Doxygen XML, and Markdown. Its [official site](https://sourcey.com/docs) describes a command-line workflow that scaffolds a project, builds HTML into `dist`, and permits hosting that output on your own infrastructure. The project identifies its license as AGPL-3.0. genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn459309018view0","turn943765928view0"]}}

This directly addresses the desired shared site and navigation. Generate the Doxygen XML from your C project, configure the documentation sources, and build the site. However, the inspected documentation emphasizes C++ examples, and I could not retrieve the detailed Doxygen and MCP adapter pages. I would check representative C functions, macros, structures, and cross-references before adopting it. Its dated changelog records the Markdown, OpenAPI, MCP, and Doxygen adapters in version 3.6.0 on May 15, 2026, before the question's cutoff. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn943765928view1"}}

### 2. MkDocs with MkDoxy, mkdocs-openapi, and an MCP export

[MkDoxy](https://mkdoxy.kubaandrysek.cz/usage/) runs Doxygen, parses its XML, and generates Markdown that participates in the MkDocs build. [mkdocs-openapi](https://pypi.org/project/mkdocs-openapi/) supplies the OpenAPI side by generating native Markdown reference pages from local OpenAPI 3.x files. The latter documents integration with navigation and search, but labels itself alpha and targets Material for MkDocs. genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn877349078view1","turn877349078view2"]}}

Add the ordinary Markdown guides and an MCP reference generated by the exporter below to the same documentation tree. This is a proposed composition of the documented components; I did not verify their combined build. It requires maintaining plugin configuration, generated-page locations, and build ordering. The exact versions and combined behavior were not established as of November 9, 2026.

### 3. Sphinx with Breathe, sphinxcontrib-openapi, MyST, and an MCP export

[Breathe](https://github.com/breathe-doc/breathe) integrates Doxygen output into Sphinx documentation. [sphinxcontrib-openapi](https://github.com/sphinx-contrib/openapi) renders an OpenAPI specification through a Sphinx directive. Sphinx's own [Markdown instructions](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/markdown.html) describe using MyST-Parser for Markdown sources. genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn238336307view0","turn877349078view3","turn238336307view1"]}}

These components provide another route to one HTML documentation tree, with the exported MCP reference included as Markdown. This requires more assembly than Sourcey: the MCP export, Doxygen generation, Sphinx extensions, and documentation navigation must be connected in the build. Check compatibility with the particular OpenAPI version and features you use. I verified the individual integration descriptions, not a complete four-input configuration.

### 4. MCP Discovery — the MCP export component

[MCP Discovery](https://docs.rs/crate/mcp-discovery/0.2.3) is an open-source CLI that inspects an MCP server and writes its capabilities to Markdown, HTML, JSON, or customizable templates. It also supports updating marked sections of existing documentation. That makes it useful for creating the MCP page consumed by either modular pipeline. Version 0.2.3 is dated January 2, 2026. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn459309018view1"}}

This is an adapter, not a complete mixed-source site generator. The export must run with access to the intended MCP server, and its output must be regenerated when the server's documented capabilities change.

### 5. mcp-docgen — another MCP-specific exporter

[mcp-docgen](https://github.com/masterthefly/mcp-docgen) documents a CLI that accepts a local MCP server project and generates HTML, Markdown, or JSON. Its Markdown output is another possible input for a shared documentation build, and the repository identifies an MIT license. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn459309018view2"}}

I did not verify its supported server implementations, transport coverage, or availability before the cutoff. Treat it as an additional exporter to evaluate, rather than an established replacement for the whole pipeline.

For the stated small project, I would start with a representative Sourcey build. If that does not handle the C output or desired presentation adequately, the two modular pipelines give concrete alternatives. For this rebuild, I would compare MediaManager with a modular Sonarr/Radarr plus Bazarr setup using the two requirements that matter most: obtaining the right subtitles for your foreign shows and reliably importing files from the seedbox. The sources below establish useful components for those jobs, but they do not demonstrate that a particular complete configuration has been deployed successfully for your collection.

## Ranked candidates

1. **Bazarr — subtitle management.** [Official setup guide](https://wiki.bazarr.media/Getting-Started/Setup-Guide/)  
   This is the most directly relevant component for the subtitle requirement. It documents language profiles, forced and hearing-impaired preferences, subtitle providers, and synchronization alongside Sonarr and Radarr. It needs access to the actual media files, and provider availability still determines which shows and languages are covered. The inspected guide is dated November 19, 2026, so its current instructions are later evidence than the January 8, 2026 question.

2. **MediaManager — the integrated option.** [Public repository](https://github.com/maxdorninger/MediaManager) · [Download-client documentation](https://maximilian-dorninger.gitbook.io/mediamanager/configuration/download-clients)  
   MediaManager offers TV and movie management in one interface. The client documentation describes qBittorrent, Transmission, and SABnzbd connections, but it also requires access to download directories; Transmission has an explicit same-path/same-volume requirement. I would therefore treat subtitle coverage and remote-file handling as acceptance tests before migration. These sources did not establish its complete foreign-subtitle workflow, and their relevant historical version dates remain unknown.

3. **Sonarr — television automation.** [Official site](https://sonarr.tv/)  
   Sonarr supplies series release selection, quality profiles, and failed-download handling. Its Docker guidance explicitly addresses consistent storage paths, permissions, and hardlinks, all relevant to retaining seeding while importing episodes. For a remote seedbox, arrange actual file access or transfer as part of the design. The live page supports these mechanisms, but I did not establish a dated version before the cutoff.

4. **SeedSync — the remote-transfer component.** [Public repository](https://github.com/ipsingh06/seedsync)  
   SeedSync runs locally and pulls files from a remote Linux server using SSH credentials and LFTP. Its pattern-based queuing and extraction can supply the missing transfer step between a seedbox and a home media server. It does not choose releases or manage subtitles, so it complements either management approach. Validate the handoff to your import process and continued seeding. The inspected README's historical availability is unverified.

5. **Radarr — the movie counterpart.** [Official site](https://radarr.video/)  
   If the collection also includes films, Radarr provides movie release selection, failed-download handling, and custom format prioritization. Its storage guidance has the same practical relevance as Sonarr's: download and library folders must be accessible with consistent paths and permissions. It adds another service and needs a subtitle component such as Bazarr. The verified page is live, with no reliable historical version date established.

6. **Medusa — an alternative integrated TV workflow.** [Official settings wiki](https://github.com/pymedusa/Medusa/wiki/Settings-explained) · [Seedbox integration guide](https://docs.seedboxes.cc/howtos/how-to-use-medusa-with-your-seedbox/)  
   Medusa combines television automation with built-in subtitle-language and provider settings. The seedbox guide describes subtitle searches and copying completed episodes while continuing to seed. This makes it a plausible third approach when reducing the number of TV-related services matters. It is TV-focused, and one provider's instructions do not prove universal seedbox compatibility. Both inspected guides carry dates before the cutoff: October 22 and September 17, 2025.

7. **Subgen — generated subtitles when providers cannot supply them.** [Public repository](https://github.com/McCloudS/subgen)  
   Subgen can produce subtitles from media audio and translate foreign speech into English, with a Bazarr integration. This addresses a different failure mode from downloading existing subtitles. It requires compute resources and a quality check on actual dialogue; arbitrary translation target languages are not established. The project's dated changelog records Bazarr support in October 2023 and language controls in December 2025. Current 2026 fixes should not be assumed available at the cutoff.

## How I would use this shortlist

My inference from the documented responsibilities is that interface consolidation alone will not settle the choice. Start with a representative foreign-language episode and an existing seedbox download. Check whether the intended subtitle language is found, whether timing is usable, whether the completed file becomes accessible to the manager, and whether importing preserves the intended seeding behavior. Repeat with a film only if films are in scope.

A modular candidate combines Sonarr for shows, Radarr if needed for movies, and Bazarr for subtitles; SeedSync is an optional transfer component when files must move from the seedbox to the local server. MediaManager deserves the same small acceptance trial because it could simplify management, while the inspected evidence leaves its subtitle and remote-storage fit unresolved. Medusa is a narrower TV alternative, and Subgen is a fallback mechanism for missing subtitle files.

This is a discovery shortlist, not a migration success claim or a finding that one application is universally better. I attempted unauthenticated native code search, which was inaccessible, and used explicitly logged code-through-web discovery instead. An initial search exposed a snippet of the excluded question thread; it was logged and excluded from evidence.

There are real alternatives to Electron, but there is no single replacement to recommend without knowing what you want to change. My first shortlist is Tauri, Wails, and Neutralinojs if keeping a web frontend matters; NW.js if retaining a Node-oriented desktop stack matters; and Flutter or Qt Quick if rebuilding the interface is acceptable. Those are selection branches, not requirements stated in your question.

I would not conclude that teams commonly return from Tauri to Electron from the evidence I found. A move from Tauri to Electron also does not, by itself, establish that the team previously used Electron and is returning to it.

## Ranked alternatives

1. **Tauri.** The closest starting point for comparing a web frontend with a Rust-backed desktop application. Its project documentation describes HTML/JavaScript/CSS frontends, a Rust backend, platform webviews, packaging, and desktop updating. It is a substantive application framework, not just a packaging trick. Test the relevant web features on each target OS before choosing it. [Project documentation](https://github.com/tauri-apps/tauri/blob/dev/README.md?plain=1)

2. **Wails.** A strong alternative when Go is a better fit for application logic. Its documented approach combines a web UI with Go methods exposed to JavaScript, desktop integration, and packaging. The inspected Wails v2 documentation uses the native rendering engine rather than embedding a browser. Consequently, switching from Tauri to Wails should not be assumed to eliminate system-webview compatibility work. The source inspected is the v2 “Next” documentation, so pin and check the release you would actually use. [Wails introduction](https://v2.wails.io/docs/next/introduction/)

3. **Neutralinojs.** Worth evaluating for a web-based desktop application whose native operations fit its APIs or extensions. It uses an existing OS browser library, with a JavaScript client and extension mechanisms. It changes the backend integration model; an Electron main process should not be assumed to migrate without adaptation. [Neutralinojs introduction](https://neutralino.js.org/docs/)

4. **NW.js.** Another desktop framework for web technologies, with documented Node.js access from the DOM and availability on Windows, macOS, and Linux. This is useful to compare when retaining Node APIs matters. I did not verify a footprint advantage, and the attempted additional getting-started page failed, so I would not select it on an assumed size or memory benefit. [NW.js](https://nwjs.io/)

5. **Flutter for desktop.** A different application stack to consider when an interface port is acceptable. The official desktop documentation covers native Windows, macOS, and Linux applications and desktop plugins. Check the plugins your application needs; do not assume an existing HTML interface transfers unchanged. [Flutter desktop documentation](https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/desktop)

6. **Qt 6 with Qt Quick.** A further option when a QML interface and C++ integration fit the team. Qt Quick documents its own visual canvas, rendering model, and UI APIs. This is a broader UI implementation choice, so budget for an interface port rather than treating it as an Electron shell substitution. I have not evaluated a particular deployment configuration or license arrangement. [Qt Quick documentation](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtquick-index.html)

All six are retained for this exploratory question. No deployment, performance, licensing, or language requirement was stated, so I have not manufactured exclusions on those grounds. Their basic implementation relationships are documented; suitability for an unspecified application is still a decision to make.

## Why a team might choose Electron after trying Tauri

Electron embeds Chromium and Node.js. Tauri uses WebView2 on Windows and WebKit-derived system components on macOS and Linux. Those are documented architecture differences. My inference is that a team can reasonably prefer controlling its bundled browser version, or preserving its Node-based application logic, over the benefits it expects from a system-webview approach. That is a tradeoff to test, not evidence of an inevitable Tauri failure. [Electron introduction](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/) · [Tauri webview reference](https://v2.tauri.app/reference/webview-versions/)

I found two useful but very different pieces of migration evidence:

- GitSquid published a first-party account dated April 21, 2026 of moving its Electron backend to Tauri/Rust while keeping most of its React frontend. That establishes a reported migration in the opposite direction; it does not establish a general success rate. [GitSquid account](https://gitsquid.dev/blog/why-we-rewrote-electron-in-tauri-rust/?article=why-we-rewrote-electron-in-tauri-rust&lang=en)
- A public mirror of OpenChamber’s commit history records a desktop cutover to Electron in May 2026 and removal of legacy Tauri support in June. The direct GitHub file attempt failed, so I treat the mirror as a provisional case record, not independently corroborated origin evidence. It also does not establish that this was a return to an earlier Electron implementation. [Mirrored commit record](https://upd.dev/btriapitsyn/openchamber/commits/branch/main/docs/TAURI_TO_ELECTRON_CUTOVER.md)

Neither provides a denominator, representative sample, or measured return rate. I therefore cannot substantiate “commonly return” from this search. The defensible conclusion is that both migration directions have public accounts or records, with different evidential strength, and that frequency remains unknown.

For an actual choice, build one representative feature in the two most relevant options. Include the native integration you expect to be hardest, the intended OS versions, packaging, and updates. Measure the resulting behavior and distribution size instead of choosing from empty-app claims. If the issue is backend language, compare Tauri with Wails; if it is the rendering model, include Electron and a different UI toolkit in the comparison.

**Evidence limit:** this was a bounded documentation review, not an implementation test or a migration survey. Most inspected documentation is live and undated; I cannot guarantee that every current detail was already present on August 28, 2026. The dated GitSquid article and the mirror’s commit dates precede that date, while the mirror snapshot itself was synchronized afterward.

I would start with **SciDAVis**, then compare **Veusz** and **LabPlot** using one of your normal datasets. **Grace** is another useful option if your work is mainly two-dimensional plots and a Unix/X11-style environment suits you. This ranking reflects fit to your plotting workflow; I did not find comparable evidence establishing which has the most academic users.

## 1. SciDAVis — my first trial for an Origin/SigmaPlot-style workflow

SciDAVis explicitly positions itself in the same application area as Origin and SigmaPlot, with a graphical interface for scientific plotting. Its repository identifies the software as GPL version 2 or later. That makes it a strong first candidate for moving your plotting work to an open-source application. Its project documentation links a manual, tutorials, forums and mailing lists, although I have not measured how quickly those channels answer questions.

Sources: [project description](https://scidavis.sourceforge.net/about/node1.html) and [official source repository](https://github.com/SciDAVis/scidavis).

## 2. Veusz — a focused graphical plotting application

Veusz is designed around producing scientific figures. You build plots from graphical elements and adjust their properties, which is a somewhat different workflow from editing a spreadsheet and selecting a chart. The current documentation lists data import, multiple plot types, error bars and vector output; its repository confirms GPL version 2 or later. A graphical interface is available even though the application also offers scripting.

The project provides a manual, examples, a tutorial, a wiki and a discussion route. I would try it when figure layout and repeatable styling are central to your work, and assess whether its editing model feels comfortable with your own data.

Sources: [overview](https://veusz.github.io/), [current repository](https://github.com/veusz/veusz), and [help resources](https://veusz.github.io/help-support/).

## 3. LabPlot — a broader graphical scientific workspace

LabPlot's official KDE page describes an open-source application that makes plots from spreadsheet data or imported files and exports figures in raster and vector formats. Its homepage describes interactive plotting with a small number of clicks. The project links discussion and support channels through KDE.

Its additional analysis facilities do not conflict with your request: you said that you do not need analysis or modeling, rather than prohibiting software that includes those functions. It deserves a trial if you prefer a data-table-and-plot workflow.

Sources: [application description](https://apps.kde.org/labplot/), [project overview](https://labplot.org/), and [support](https://labplot.org/pages/support/).

## 4. Grace — particularly relevant for 2D plots on Unix-like systems

Grace's official site describes a point-and-click 2D plotting application, with graph customization and export options. Its license link points to the GNU GPL. The site also links a user guide, tutorial, FAQ and forums.

The platform fit needs attention: the official description focuses on Unix/X11 and refers to older Windows ports. Because you did not specify an operating system, I would keep it on the shortlist while checking installation on your actual machine. I am recommending it for 2D scientific plots, with no claim that it reproduces every Surfer or Origin feature.

Sources: [Grace overview and help links](https://plasma-gate.weizmann.ac.il/Grace/) and [linked license](https://plasma-gate.weizmann.ac.il/Grace/doc/GPL.html).

## Choosing between them

For a useful trial, import a representative dataset, reproduce a figure you already know, adjust its axes and labels, and save/export it. This will expose the practical differences in ease of use and your required plot types. My first two trials would be SciDAVis and Veusz; LabPlot is also a strong direct match.

These recommendations come from project documentation; I have not performed hands-on academic use for this answer. Public help routes are documented, but a reliable popularity ordering and response-rate comparison remain unverified.

**Date qualification:** Your question is dated 26 October 2016. Several opened sources describe later software: SciDAVis's mission page is dated April 2017, Veusz's opened repository describes version 4.2.1, and LabPlot's current pages include 2025–2026 material. An [official July 2016 LabPlot announcement](https://labplot.org/posts/windows-version-of-labplot-is-comming-soon/) describes Windows installers as forthcoming with version 2.3.0 and a Mac port as planned. The current feature and platform lists therefore should not be treated as a verified reconstruction of the exact choices available in October 2016.

## Recommendation

Start with **TheirStack**, and compare it with **PredictLeads** on a small set of companies you already understand. They are the strongest documented matches I found for preparing consultancy sales conversations from company technology signals. **HG Insights** is a broader enterprise alternative. **Sumble** and **Enlyft** are worth follow-up, but my document access was not sufficient to verify them to the same standard.

The key distinction for this use case is the evidence behind each claim. A technology mentioned in a job advertisement can be a useful opening for a conversation, but it does not establish that the company currently deploys it throughout the organization. Treat a returned stack as a set of research leads, with dates and source context.

### 1. TheirStack — first choice for the stated emphasis

TheirStack's official guide explicitly covers CI/CD and security tools, including examples such as Okta, CrowdStrike, Splunk, and Vault. Its company-technographics endpoint returns confidence levels, job-mention counts, and first/last mention dates; its documented filters let you select confidence levels, categories, and recency. This makes it a practical first API to evaluate for your use case.

Sources: [internal-stack guide](https://theirstack.com/en/docs/guides/how-to-discover-tech-stack-of-any-company) and [API reference](https://theirstack.com/en/docs/api-reference/companies/technographics_v1).

I would begin with recent, higher-confidence signals and inspect the underlying context before phrasing a sales question as an established fact. The documented fit is strong; I have not tested its accuracy on your accounts.

### 2. PredictLeads — strongest alternative for inspecting detection evidence

PredictLeads documents a company technology-detections endpoint and an extended-detection endpoint. The latter exposes the clues behind a detection, including job, webpage, DNS, and connection evidence; the data model includes first/last seen dates and source counts. That is particularly useful when your previous failure was an unsupported stack assertion.

Source: [Technology Detections API and data model](https://docs.predictleads.com/v3/guide/technology_detections_dataset/api_endpoints).

Check the particular CI/CD and security products you care about in a sample. I verified the documented evidence workflow, not coverage or present deployment at any specific company.

### 3. HG Insights — broader enterprise alternative

HG documents technographic company enrichment by domain, with installation-related metadata. Its methodology article describes combining company-produced documents with digital signals and retaining verification dates. That is a plausible alternative when you need wider enterprise account intelligence.

Sources: [company enrichment API](https://data-docs.hginsights.com/v2/guides/enrichment) and [installation methodology](https://support.hginsights.com/articles/6696649277-introduction-to-technology-installs).

Ask for a sample containing the exact CI/CD and security tools and target companies relevant to your consultancy. The public documentation supports the API research workflow; it does not establish those specific coverage or purchasing details. Also, the [API overview](https://help.hginsights.com/docs/hg-api) was updated after the question date, so the current documentation should not be read as a complete record of what was available in July 2026.

### 4. Sumble — promising, with verification still needed

Official indexed documentation describes organization technology enrichment and job-based account evidence. However, the opened API and methodology pages exposed only documentation pointers in this run. I would retain Sumble as an evaluation option, conditional on confirming its endpoint schemas, evidence access, and coverage of your relevant technologies.

Sources: [API documentation](https://docs.sumble.com/api) and [data methodology](https://docs.sumble.com/our-data). These are preliminary leads from official search excerpts, not fully verified opened-body evidence.

### 5. Enlyft — another option to verify

Official search results identify a public API and a technology-lookup capability through its MCP documentation. The REST page returned no readable body, and the opened MCP excerpt only established setup/authentication. It therefore remains a follow-up candidate, rather than an equally verified recommendation.

Sources: [public API documentation](https://docs.enlyft.com/) and [MCP documentation](https://mcp.enlyft.com/docs).

## How I would choose

Run the same small account set through the leading candidates, using companies whose stack you can independently check. Evaluate useful CI/CD/security detections, source traceability, observation dates, company matching, and false positives. Include a few companies with little public hiring to expose coverage gaps. This is a proposed evaluation method, not a benchmark I performed.

For the eventual sales brief, retain the technology, observation date, source reference, and uncertainty. A question such as “I saw a recent role mentioning Jenkins; is that still part of your delivery setup?” uses the signal without turning inference into fact. You can then use an LLM to organize supplied evidence while requiring unsupported claims to remain unknown.

No explicit price, platform, license, or no-AI prohibition was present in the supplied summary, so I did not exclude products on those grounds. Prices and actual API results were not tested. Research used live public material on November 21, 2026; undated pages are marked unknown, and observed later revisions are marked post-decision. The original question thread and its answers were not used.

There are several credible ways to get an open-weight alternative to the Claude Code workflow. I would first try Qwen Code with a Qwen3-Coder backend for an integrated terminal coding setup, or goose with a suitable local model if coding is only part of the intended use. OpenCode is another useful starting point when choosing the terminal interface and the model independently matters.

The wording can reasonably refer to the terminal agent, the model behind it, or both. These are separate pieces: an open-source command-line tool can still call a closed hosted model, while an open-weight model needs a harness to read files, execute tools, and maintain a working session. The following options cover both interpretations without assuming which one was intended.

1. Qwen Code — https://github.com/QwenLM/qwen-code
Qwen Code is an open-source terminal agent designed alongside Qwen3-Coder. The original July 22, 2025 announcement introduced the model and CLI together, making this the clearest integrated candidate in the sources inspected. Its current repository describes multiple model protocols and local backends through Ollama or vLLM. Configure an open-weight backend deliberately: installing the CLI alone does not establish that the inference is local or uses open weights. The newer repository features are live documentation rather than a historical snapshot.

2. OpenCode with a local model — https://opencode.ai/docs/models
OpenCode lets the terminal workflow use models served by Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, or a compatible endpoint. This is a practical harness option if the main attraction of Claude Code is interactive work in a terminal while retaining control of the model. A suitable model and serving configuration still matter: the documentation explicitly notes extra configuration for vLLM tool calling. I have not established the exact availability of the current integration features before the question date.

3. goose — https://goose-docs.ai/
goose is particularly relevant to the phrase “coding and other tasks.” Its official site describes a general-purpose agent with a CLI, local-model support, reusable recipes, and MCP tool extensions, with examples spanning research, writing, data analysis, automation, and coding. That breadth makes it a strong alternative mechanism to investigate. Actual task coverage depends on the chosen model and enabled tools. The current homepage is undated, so its exact feature set should not be treated as a verified November 1 snapshot.

4. Aider with Ollama — https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider/blob/main/aider/website/docs/llms/ollama.md
Aider provides a concrete terminal coding workflow with locally served models. Its own public documentation shows selecting an Ollama model and connecting it to a codebase, and discusses context-window settings. It is a focused choice for coding assistance; the evidence inspected does not establish it as an equally broad replacement for arbitrary non-coding work. Small or incompatible models and insufficient context may limit the experience.

5. Open Interpreter — https://github.com/openinterpreter/openinterpreter
The current project provides a terminal agent with selectable model harnesses, OpenAI-compatible providers, native command sandboxing, and browser/native-interface QA support. Its harness-emulation approach is useful when the best workflow for a chosen open model differs from a generic prompt-and-tools loop. The current repository describes a substantially evolved implementation; I would not assume that today's behavior or model support matches older descriptions. The viewed evidence is undated and does not verify the exact pre-question release.

6. Qwen3-Coder, as the model component — https://qwenlm.github.io/blog/qwen3-coder/
If “open-weight alternative” primarily means a model, Qwen3-Coder is a concrete option. The dated official announcement provides weight links and describes coding, browser-use, and tool-use objectives, together with the companion Qwen Code CLI. The announced 480B-total-parameter model is a substantial serving commitment. It is a model component rather than a complete terminal application, and I have not independently verified the vendor's comparative performance claims.

For a first trial, pair one harness with one explicitly identified open-weight model and compare it on representative coding and non-coding tasks from the intended workflow. Qwen Code is the most directly paired option in these sources; goose is the strongest explicit fit for broad everyday tasks; OpenCode offers a clearly documented route to choosing the local backend separately. None of these sources establishes that a particular pairing will match Claude Code's reliability on every task.

Evidence limitations: these are public primary-source checks, not hands-on tests. The Qwen announcement is dated July 22, 2025; the other current documentation pages have unverified historical dates. Unauthenticated GitHub code search failed with DisabledError, so the code-source lookup used a web search restricted to public GitHub /blob/ content. The initial Open Interpreter website fetch had no readable body; its official repository supplied the usable evidence instead. No source-thread answers or recognized copies of the excluded question were used.

For this home-lab workflow, I would first evaluate Fabric if the aim is to preserve the existing sequence of copying files and running commands. If a browser interface and retained run logs are central requirements, Semaphore UI is a useful next option. These are fit judgments based on the public documentation, not results from deploying the tools.

1. **Fabric — closest match to the existing workflow.** Its [upstream getting-started guide](https://github.com/fabric/fabric/blob/main/sites/docs/getting-started.rst) demonstrates an archive upload followed by a remote unpack command. Remote output is printed and captured, with exit status available to the calling program. A Python task could package the source, upload it and execute the existing commands. Scheduling, a web interface and durable run history would require additional work.

2. **pyinfra — useful when deployment also changes host state.** The [getting-started guide](https://docs.pyinfra.com/en/3.x/getting-started.html) describes reusable Python deployments, SSH inventories and commands whose output is displayed. Its [file operations](https://docs.pyinfra.com/en/3.x/operations/files.html) provide uploads. This could combine source distribution with package, service or configuration changes. Ordinary commands still need deliberate repeat-run behavior, and the documented files.put operation has a large-file caveat.

3. **Ansible — a structured way to express transfer and execution.** The [copy module](https://docs.ansible.com/projects/ansible/latest/collections/ansible/builtin/copy_module.html) can transfer a directory tree, while the [script module](https://docs.ansible.com/projects/ansible/latest/collections/ansible/builtin/script_module.html) uploads and runs a local script. A playbook can therefore represent the current steps explicitly. The script module's SSH pseudo-terminal combines stderr with stdout; the documentation recommends copy plus command when preserving separate output streams matters.

4. **Semaphore UI — useful for launching automation and reviewing its runs.** Its [quickstart](https://semaphoreui.com/docs/getting-started) describes Git-backed automation, credentials, execution environments and retained status and logs. It could put an interface around an Ansible deployment or an existing script workflow. The actual transfer and execution logic still needs to be supplied, and the service or runner needs the relevant execution tools.

5. **Rundeck — a job-oriented transfer-and-execute mechanism.** Its [file-copier documentation](https://docs.rundeck.com/docs/developer/file-copier-plugins.html) describes sending a script to a node, executing it through a node executor and streaming results back. That directly addresses remote commands and their output. Moving an entire application source tree requires an explicit packaging, synchronization or checkout step beyond the documented script-dispatch mechanism.

6. **SSHKit — a compact Ruby toolkit for the same workflow.** The [upstream examples](https://github.com/capistrano/sshkit/blob/master/EXAMPLES.md) cover recursive file uploads, command execution, captured output and logging configuration, using SCP or SFTP for transfers. It is a reasonable component when Ruby is comfortable and a small custom deployment program is desirable. The user must still define task ordering and handle command context and failures.

7. **Dokku — an alternative when the real goal is deploying an application.** Its [architecture documentation](https://dokku.com/docs/development/architecture/) describes receiving a Git push, building a Docker image and deploying containers. Its [log-management documentation](https://dokku.com/docs/deployment/logs/) provides live application output and failed-deployment logs. This changes the deployment model more substantially than a scripting toolkit; retaining logs from older deployments requires additional persistence.

The main choice is whether the desired result is a repeatable command-line task, a centrally managed job with a user interface, or an application deployment platform. The first two remain close to the existing SSH-based workflow; Dokku is a plausible alternative when application lifecycle management is useful.

Research limits: these candidates were checked against live primary documentation and public source examples. I did not establish dated versions of the inspected content before the 2026-06-18 cutoff, so all evidence is marked date_status=unknown rather than assumed historical. The unauthenticated grep.app attempt was inaccessible; the subsequent SSHKit search used public code indexed by web search and is explicitly recorded as code-through-web. No tool was installed or deployed, and no source-thread answers were consulted.

It can make sense to switch, but the repeated outages in your description are a reason to evaluate a move, not enough evidence to identify a more reliable provider. I would first identify what actually stops you working: fetching code, pushing changes, reviewing contributions, running CI, or publishing releases. The best alternative depends on that boundary.

My practical recommendation is to test GitLab.com with one representative repository and maintain an independent copy of your Git data during the evaluation. For a qualifying free-software project, Codeberg is also a serious hosted option. Forgejo and SourceHut become more attractive when their operating or collaboration model suits you.

## Ranked options

1. **GitLab.com — the first general hosted alternative to evaluate.** GitLab documents importing GitHub projects, including collaboration records, but the importer does not bring over GitHub organizations or groups. Check its permissions and import limitations before trusting a migration. GitLab also publishes a separate guide for converting GitHub Actions workflows into GitLab CI/CD, so CI should be tested as its own migration task. This is a documented route to another host, not evidence that its uptime will be better for your workload. [GitHub importer](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/import/github/); [CI migration](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/migration/github_actions/). genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn113172141view0","turn250146023view0","turn287527577view3"]}}

2. **Keep GitHub and add an independent Git mirror — useful if code access is the immediate problem.** GitHub documents maintaining a mirror by cloning and periodically pushing to another location; Git LFS objects have additional transfer steps. My suggested adaptation is to choose a destination independent of GitHub, establish an update schedule, and test that you can fetch from it. A mirror covers repository history. It is not, by itself, a replacement for your issue tracker, reviews, CI, releases, or an agreed write-failover process. It also cannot contain changes that have not reached it. [Mirroring guide](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/duplicating-a-repository). genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn287527577view2"}}

3. **Codeberg — evaluate for free-software work.** Codeberg is a non-profit, Forgejo-based hosting service. Its suitability depends on your project: the FAQ distinguishes its free-software mission from general private commercial hosting, with limited private-content exceptions. It also describes resource and CI access requests. Since you did not specify the repository type, I would keep Codeberg on the shortlist while confirming eligibility. [Overview](https://docs.codeberg.org/getting-started/what-is-codeberg/); [FAQ](https://docs.codeberg.org/getting-started/faq/). genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn113172141view2","turn287527577view0"]}}

4. **Self-hosted Forgejo — evaluate if you want to operate the host.** Forgejo supplies a self-hosted alternative, giving you a direct choice of infrastructure and operation. My inference is that this changes who carries the hosting work; it does not automatically improve availability. You would need a workable plan for updates, recovery, monitoring and any CI runners. Its v15.0 Actions documentation explicitly distinguishes familiarity with GitHub Actions from compatibility, so test your actual workflows. You have not stated whether self-hosting is acceptable, which is the main unresolved choice here. [Forgejo](https://forgejo.org/); [Actions differences](https://forgejo.org/docs/v15.0/user/actions/github-actions/). genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn250146023view4","turn250146023view2"]}}

5. **SourceHut — evaluate if its collaboration model appeals to you.** SourceHut documents hosted Git repositories, CI, issue tracking, and mailing-list/patch-based review. That makes it a real alternative, but the workflow needs to work for your contributors. The current homepage calls it a public alpha. I would run a small review-and-build trial before moving an established project; this research does not establish complete GitHub metadata migration or a measured availability improvement. [SourceHut features](https://sourcehut.org/). genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn287527577view1"}}

## How I would decide whether the move is worth it

Treat the migration as a small experiment. Pick a representative repository and list the things it actually depends on: contributors' access, review process, automation, deployment credentials, packages, large files and documentation. Check the imported result, run the build and release path, and have someone other than the administrator try contributing. These are suggested evaluation criteria, not requirements you already stated.

Then compare the cost of the interruptions you experience with the migration effort and the continuing cost of the new setup. If the current interruptions regularly block necessary work and a pilot succeeds, moving is reasonable. If the main need is occasional access to code while the rest of your workflow remains strongly tied to GitHub, an independent mirror may provide useful resilience with a smaller change. If CI is the bottleneck, test an independent build path rather than assuming a change of repository URL solves it.

I have not compared provider incident histories over the same period or established a reliability ranking. Nor have I assumed a budget, a preferred review process, use of GitHub Actions, or willingness to self-host. The evidence above is documentation, not an executed migration. Most pages are live and undated; they support a current shortlist, but do not prove the exact feature or policy state on the question date, 17 August 2026.
